entries.title: WWF King of the Ring
entries.summary: LJN's 1993 WWF game, the last WWF release for the NES: win an eight-man King of the Ring elimination tournament, or beat the whole roster in singles matches for the WWF title.
entries.why_it_matters: The final WWF game released on the NES, and the last NES/Game Boy game made by Gray Matter.
entries.gameplay_notes: Eleven wrestlers, including The Undertaker and Bam Bam Bigelow (both missing from the Game Boy version) and a custom wrestler you name and give attributes. Everyone shares the same basic moveset with no signature moves; wrestlers differ only in speed, strength and stamina. Exhibition singles and tag matches support one or two players.

entries.title: WWF WrestleMania
entries.summary: Rare's 1989 WrestleMania for Acclaim, the first WWF-licensed NES game, released months before WrestleMania V.
entries.why_it_matters: Started Acclaim's roughly decade-long relationship with the WWF; the first of Rare's two NES WWF games.
entries.gameplay_notes: Six wrestlers (Hogan, André the Giant, Savage, DiBiase, Bigelow, Honky Tonk Man) with small, slightly tailored movesets; no leaving the ring. A wrestler who turns red is angry and hits harder, and each has a personal health icon only they can collect. Tournament mode takes up to six players in a round robin (15 matches), ties broken by fastest win.

entries.title: WWF WrestleMania Challenge
entries.summary: Rare's 1990 WWF game for LJN (developed as WWF Survivor Series), viewed from a high isometric angle with nine wrestlers.
entries.why_it_matters: Rare's second and last NES WWF game; later WrestleMania titles moved to Sculptured Software.
entries.gameplay_notes: Modes: one-on-one, tag team, three-on-three Survivor Series elimination, a championship played as the generic 'Yourself' wrestler, and a two-player tag championship. Stamina bars sit on the ring apron; an empty bar leaves you open to pinfalls.

entries.title: Xenophobe
entries.summary: Sunsoft's NES port of Bally Midway's 1987 arcade game: clear alien-infested space stations before the countdown runs out.
entries.gameplay_notes: Aliens mature through stages (Pod, Critter, Rollerbaby, Snotterpillar) if left alone. Stations span several floors linked by elevators. A mission ends by clearing all aliens, by self-destructing the station after enough kills, or by running out of time. NES-specific differences are not documented in the source.

entries.title: Xevious
entries.summary: Bandai's NES release of Namco's Famicom Xevious: the 1983 vertical shooter in which the Solvalou uses an air zapper and a ground blaster.
entries.why_it_matters: The Famicom version (1984) was one of the system's first third-party games; the arcade original set the template for vertically scrolling shooters.
entries.gameplay_notes: Shoot air targets and bomb ground targets through a reticle ahead of the ship; hidden towers can be uncovered by bombing specific spots. The source describes the arcade game's structure; NES-specific changes are not detailed.

entries.title: Xexyz
entries.summary: Atlus/Hudson Soft's 1988 game (NA April 1990) alternating side-scrolling platform stages with Gradius-style shooter stages, set on a post-apocalyptic island in 2777.
entries.gameplay_notes: As Apollo, collect currency from enemies in platform stages to spend at hidden shops and minigames; in shooter stages, 'S' and 'P' items upgrade speed and weapons.
entries.hltb_note: HLTB NES platform row (6 completions logged; Wikidata-linked)
entries.collecting_notes: Released in Japan and North America only; no PAL release. The Famicom original has an Urashima Tarō theme, cutscenes and three endings.

entries.title: Yo! Noid
entries.summary: Capcom's 1990 Domino's Pizza tie-in, localised from Now Production's Kamen no Ninja Hanamaru: the Noid crosses New York to stop his green double, Mr. Green.
entries.gameplay_notes: One-hit deaths and a per-level time limit. The yo-yo is your weapon; collected scrolls fuel screen-clearing magic. Some levels use a skateboard or autogyro. Bosses are pizza-eating contests instead of Hanamaru's card battles.

entries.title: Yoshi
entries.summary: Game Freak's falling-block puzzler for Nintendo (NA 1992): Mario swaps four columns so falling Mario enemies land on matching pieces, and joined eggshell halves hatch Yoshis.
entries.why_it_matters: Game Freak's first game with Nintendo, helping fund the company on the road to Pokémon.
entries.gameplay_notes: NES stacks hold up to eight pieces (seven on Game Boy). Enclosing monsters between a bottom and top eggshell clears them all and hatches a bigger Yoshi. Single-player score play plus a competitive two-player mode.

entries.title: Yoshi's Cookie

entries.gameplay_notes: Cookies keep arriving from the top and right; the game ends if the grid overflows. A Yoshi-head cookie acts as a wild card.

entries.title: The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles
entries.summary: Jaleco's December 1992 side-scrolling action game based on the TV series: eight levels across Mexico, France and Germany, from the Mexican Civil War to World War I.
entries.gameplay_notes: Weapons and items double as health: each hit costs a possession, and when empty you fight bare-fisted and die on the next hit. Picked-up weapons (dynamite, daggers, grenades, guns) replace the whip. Early levels follow TV episodes; later ones tell an original story, including a Red Baron dogfight.

entries.title: Zanac
entries.summary: Compile's vertical shooter (NES 1987, published by FCI): twelve areas of fast shooting to destroy the System, an alien machine bent on wiping out humanity.
entries.why_it_matters: Noted for adaptive difficulty that reacts to your skill, rate of fire and defences; by the Compile core team behind The Guardian Legend and Blazing Lazers.
entries.gameplay_notes: Blue boxes upgrade the main cannon; numbered power-ups select one of eight special weapons, or upgrade it if the number matches. Dying loses all power-ups. Boss fortresses are turret clusters to destroy against a timer. Continues restart the current area.

difficulty.reason: Known for its difficulty and dense enemy fire (GameSpot, Allgame).

entries.title: Zelda II: The Adventure of Link
entries.summary: Nintendo's 1987 sequel (NES December 1988): Link seeks the Triforce of Courage to wake a long-sleeping Princess Zelda, mixing a top-down overworld with side-scrolling towns, caves and palaces.
entries.why_it_matters: The series' most unusual main entry, with experience points, lives and spells; it introduced the magic meter and Dark Link.
entries.gameplay_notes: Side-view sword combat, experience levels, spells learned from townsfolk, and a lives system. Set crystals in six palaces to open the Great Palace.

entries.title: Zoda's Revenge: StarTropics II
entries.summary: Nintendo's 1994 StarTropics sequel: Mike Jones travels through history, from the Stone Age to Victorian England, collecting Tetrads and defeating three clones of Zoda.
entries.why_it_matters: The last game Nintendo developed exclusively for the NES, and its second-to-last first-party NES release.
entries.gameplay_notes: Nine chapters with heart-container health. Mike moves in eight directions and can steer mid-jump. New weapons come from historical figures, and Merlin teaches an upgradable psychic shock wave whose power scales with hearts.

entries.title: Zombie Nation
entries.summary: KAZe/Meldac's shooter: the giant flying samurai head Namakubi fires eyeballs and vomit to wreck zombified American cities and reclaim the sword Shura from Darc Seed.
entries.gameplay_notes: Pick any of four stages to start, then play the rest in sequence. An eight-unit life bar refills by destroying things; rescued zombie hostages boost firepower. Easy and hard settings. Getting crushed by the scrolling screen is instant death.
